newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia Svyazinvest winner may get more board seats.
newsitem.headline: Russia Svyazinvest winner may get more board seats.

text.p: The winner of an auction for a 25 percent plus one share stake in Russian telecoms holding company Svyazinvest could be given a disproportionately large number of board seats, a senior government communications official said.

First deputy communications minister Valentin Boldin told Reuters that the government was also preparing a plan for a $2-$3 billion investment programme that would be ready by the time a second stake of 24 percent of the company was sold.
"Why shouldn't the Russian side give (the winner) not two but three or four (seats)?" Boldin said in an interview late on Monday.

There are nine seats on the board of directors of the holding company, which owns controlling stakes in 88 regional and other telecoms companies. "If they are good specialists and theirs are better than ours, then why not?" he said.

Boldin said the government would maintain control of Svyazinvest and would dismiss any member of the board who became an obstacle to government policy. "The shareholders' meeting is every year and if need be we will call one every month," he said.

Five seats on the board were held by representatives of the Ministry of Communications -- which is in the process of becoming a committee -- the Antimonopoly Committee, the State Property Committee, the Federal Agency for Government Communications and Svyazinvest itself, he said.

The sale of the Svyazinvest stake has raised confusion in the telecommunications industry over whether Russia is looking for a strategic partner to help guide Svyazinvest, seen as a key to telecoms industry's development, or only a source of funds.
"Considering the amount of money we have asked for, it is difficult to think a single investor will be found with $1.2 billion to invest," Boldin said.
"I do not at all dismiss the possibility that it will be a Russian and Western investors including operators and even pension funds."

He added that any Western partner taking part in the group with the successful bid would be able to get a domestic operating licence from the communications body. "Our legislation is such that it is easier for us to take away a licence than to not give it," he said.
Ninety-five percent of the proceeds from the first auction will go straight into the federal treasury but the second auction is expected to have a large investment component.

Boldin said a $2-$3 billion investment programme would be prepared by the time of the 24 percent stake. "We have already nearly worked out an investment programme for communications in Russia, and in around four to five months it will be ready," Boldin said.

"At the same time we will start the second phase of privatisation (of Svyazinvest), and will sell 24 percent," he said. "It (the programme) is ready in rough form already, but we want to develop it to standards seen in the West. It will involve not less than $2-3 billion," Boldin said.
He said the investments would be used to boost the capacity of telephone lines and to transfer regional electronic communications systems into a digital communications system.
